text: The science of politics, however, like most other sciences, has received great improvement.
locator: Alexander Hamilton, No. 9

text: As long as the reason of man continues fallible, and he is at liberty to exercise it, different opinions will be formed.

text: When the sword is once drawn, the passions of men observe no bounds of moderation.
locator: Alexander Hamilton, No. 16

text: Each circle is the miniature picture of the deformities of this political monster.

text: Experience is the oracle of truth; and where its responses are unequivocal, they ought to be conclusive and sacred.
locator: James Madison, No. 20

text: Though a wide ocean separates the United States from Europe, yet there are various considerations that warn us against an excess of confidence or security.
locator: Alexander Hamilton, No. 24

text: Man is very much a creature of habit.
locator: Alexander Hamilton, No. 27

text: What is a power, but the ability or faculty of doing a thing?
locator: Alexander Hamilton, No. 33

text: A bad cause seldom fails to betray itself.

text: When men exercise their reason coolly and freely on a variety of distinct questions, they inevitably fall into different opinions on some of them. When they are governed by a common passion, their opinions, if they are so to be called, will be the same.
locator: James Madison, No. 50

text: If men were angels, no government would be necessary.
locator: James Madison, No. 51

text: With less power, therefore, to abuse, the federal representatives can be less tempted on one side, and will be doubly watched on the other.
locator: James Madison, No. 52

locator: James Madison, No. 54

locator: James Madison, No. 58

text: The constitutional possibility of the thing, without an equivalent for the risk, is an unanswerable objection.
locator: Alexander Hamilton, No. 59

text: The interest of all would, in this respect at least, be the security of all.
locator: Alexander Hamilton, No. 60

locator: Alexander Hamilton, No. 73

locator: Alexander Hamilton, No. 77

text: That there ought to be one court of supreme and final jurisdiction, is a proposition which is not likely to be contested.
locator: Alexander Hamilton, No. 81

text: I never expect to see a perfect work from imperfect man.
locator: Alexander Hamilton, No. 85

text: Your right to swing your arms ends just where the other man's nose begins.
locator: "Freedom of Speech in Wartime", 32 Harvard Law Review 932, 957 (1919). (Various permutations of this quote have been incorrectly attributed to Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr.). "Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores, Inc." dissent by Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg.

text: That's too civil by half.
locator: Robert Brinsley Sheridan, The Rivals (1775), Act III, scene 4.

text: A blush is no language: only a dubious flag-signal which may mean either of two contradictories.
locator: George Eliot, Daniel Deronda (1876), Book V, Chapter XXXV.

text: Thus we see, too, in the world that some persons assimilate only what is ugly and evil from the same moral circumstances which supply good and beautiful results—the fragrance of celestial flowers—to the daily life of others.
locator: Nathaniel Hawthorne, Mosses from an Old Manse, The Old Manse

text: Good deeds remain good, no matter whether we know how the world was made or not. Vile deeds are vile, no matter whether we know or do not know what, after death, will be the fate of the doer.
locator: Felix Adler, Life and Destiny (1913), Section 9 : Ethical Outlook

text: Discontent is the first step in the progress of a man or a nation.
locator: Oscar Wilde, A Woman of No Importance (1893), Act II.

text: Extremes meet, and there is no better example than the haughtiness of humility.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Letters and Social Aims (1876), Greatness

text: Hugh laughed again, and with such thorough abandonment to his mad humour, that his limbs seemed dislocated, and his whole frame in danger of tumbling to pieces; but Mr Tappertit, so far from receiving this extreme merriment with any irritation, was pleased to regard it with the utmost favour, and even to join in it, so far as one of his gravity and station could, with any regard to that decency and decorum which men in high places are expected to maintain.
locator: Charles Dickens, Barnaby Rudge (1841).

text: A mere madness, to live like a wretch, and die rich.
locator: Robert Burton, The Anatomy of Melancholy (1621), Part I, Section II. Memb. 3. Subsec. 13.

text: It was a night so beautiful that your soul seemed hardly able to bear the prison of the body.
locator: W. Somerset Maugham, The Moon and Sixpence (1919), ch. 53

text: The longest way must have its close,—the gloomiest night will wear on to a morning.
locator: Harriet Beecher Stowe, Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852), vol. 2, ch. 40

text: They lard their lean books with the fat of others' works.
locator: Robert Burton, The Anatomy of Melancholy (1621), Democritus to the Reader.

text: Consequences are unpitying. Our deeds carry their terrible consequences, quite apart from any fluctuations that went before—consequences that are hardly ever confined to ourselves.
locator: George Eliot, Adam Bede, Chapter XVI. in Hoyt's New Cyclopedia Of Practical Quotations (1922), p. 670

text: Now, so far as I can judge, self-love is the root of all evil;
locator: Helen Keller, The Story of My Life. (AmazonClassics Edition) p. 104.

text: So she poured out the liquid music of her voice to quench the thirst of his spirit.
locator: Nathaniel Hawthorne, Mosses from an Old Manse, The Birthmark.

text: The shoemaker makes a good shoe because he makes nothing else.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Letters and Social Aims (1876), Greatness.

text: In came Mrs. Fezziwig, one vast substantial smile.
locator: Charles Dickens, A Christmas Carol (1843), Stave 2.

text: When the military man approaches, the world locks up its spoons and packs off its womankind.
locator: Bernard Shaw, Man and Superman.

text: The gratitude of most men is but a secret desire of receiving greater benefits.
locator: François de La Rochefoucauld, Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims, Maxim 298 (1665–1678).

text: Women have, commonly, a very positive moral sense; that which they will, is right; that which they reject, is wrong; and their will, in most cases, ends by settling the moral.
locator: Henry Adams, The Education of Henry Adams (1918), ch. 6

text: Forward and backward all in one; that is the way she loves to be wooed. She is a woman, remember that.
locator: Robert Hugh Benson, By What Authority? (1905), pt. 2, ch. 9

text: It's queer how out of touch with truth women are. They live in a world of their own, and there has never been anything like it, and never can be. It is too beautiful altogether, and if they were to set it up it would go to pieces before the first sunset. Some confounded fact we men have been living contentedly with ever since the day of creation would start up and knock the whole thing over.
locator: Joseph Conrad, Heart of Darkness (1902)

text: A woman will always sacrifice herself if you give her the opportunity. It is her favourite form of self-indulgence.
locator: W. Somerset Maugham, The Circle (1921), act 3 (Champion-Cheney loq.)

text: Oh! no one. No one in particular. A woman of no importance.
locator: Oscar Wilde, A Woman of No Importance (1893), act 1

text: Why don't you speak for yourself, John?
locator: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, The Courtship of Miles Standish (1858), III. Last line.

text: When an actor has money, he doesn't send letters but telegrams.
locator: Anton Chekhov, Note-Book of Anton Chekhov.

text: No affectation of peculiarity can conceal a commonplace mind.
locator: Somerset Maugham, The Moon and Sixpence (1919), Ch. 42.

text: The highest form of vanity is love of fame.
locator: George Santayana, The Life of Reason: The Phases of Human Progress (1906)

text: It was the beginning of a day in June; the deep blue sky unsullied by a cloud, and teeming with brilliant light. The streets were, as yet, nearly free from passengers, the houses and shops were closed, and the healthy air of morning fell like breath from angels, on the sleeping town.
locator: Charles Dickens in The Old Curiosity Shop (1841).

text: In aesthetic theory it might be extremely difficult, if not quite impracticable, to draw a line between the canon of classicism, or regard for the archaic, and the canon of beauty.
locator: Thorstein Veblen, The Theory of the Leisure Class: An Economic Study of Institutions (1899).

text: She had gained a reputation for beauty, and (which is often another thing) was beautiful.
locator: Charles Dickens, Little Dorrit (1855–57)

text: There is a great deal of difference between the eager man who wants to read a book, and the tired man who wants a book to read.
locator: G. K. Chesterton, Charles Dickens (1906).

text: There are two motives for reading a book: one, that you enjoy it; the other, that you can boast about it.
locator: Bertrand Russell, The Conquest of Happiness (1930), Ch. 3: Competition.

text: In every man's memory, with the hours when life culminated are usually associated certain books which met his views.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Letters and Social Aims (1876), Quotation and Originality.

text: We prize books, and they prize them most who are themselves wise.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Letters and Social Aims (1876), Quotation and Originality.

text: You can hardly have too much harmony in business. But you can go too far in picking men because they harmonize.
locator: Henry Ford (1863-1947), American automobile industrialist. 'Democracy and industry', Chapter XVIII, My Life and Work (1922), written in collaboration with Samuel Crowther.

text: Some day the ethics of business will be universally recognized, and in that day business will be seen to be the oldest and most useful of all the professions.
locator: Henry Ford. 'What we may expect', Chapter XIX, My Life and Work (1922), written in collaboration with Samuel Crowther.

text: A merry Christmas to everybody! A happy New Year to all the world!
locator: Charles Dickens in A Christmas Carol

text: I've never any pity for conceited people, because I think they carry their comfort about with them.
locator: George Eliot, The Mill on the Floss (1860), Book V, Chapter IV.

text: The people must be helped to think naturally about money. They must be told what it is, and what makes it money, and what are the possible tricks of the present system which put nations and peoples under control of the few.
locator: Henry Ford, My Life and Work, Doubleday, Page & Company, 1922, p. 179

text: The most difficult crime to track is the one which is purposeless.
locator: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle (1859-1930), British crime novelist. Sherlock Holmes, in "The Naval Treaty," The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes (1892).

text: Envy is the basis of democracy.
locator: Bertrand Russell, The Conquest of Happiness (1930), Ch. VI

text: If either the absence or the presence of novelty is equally annoying, it would hardly seem that either could be the true cause of despair.
locator: Bertrand Russell, The Conquest of Happiness (1930), Chapter 2: Byronic Unhappiness.
